knownFor.label: Sankore & Timbuktu scholars
knownFor.note: Timbuktu’s mosques and scholars made it a centre of Islamic learning.

knownFor.label: Askia Muhammad
knownFor.note: Reformed government and made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca.

knownFor.label: Niger river fleet
knownFor.note: Canoe fleets that controlled the Niger river.

location.value: The western Sahel along the Niger River, centred on Gao. At its peak it was one of the largest African empires in history.

terrain.value: The Niger bend, the Sahel and the southern Sahara.

climate.value: Sahel climate: hot, with a short rainy season, along the Niger River.

resources.value: Gold, salt (the Taghaza mines), river farming and fishing.

disasters.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

population.value: No reliable figure; perhaps a few million at its height.

urbanisation.value: Gao (capital), Timbuktu (conquered 1468) and Djenné (1473/1475) were great trading and scholarly cities.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: After 1591 Songhai nobles moved south into present-day Niger (the Dendi kingdom).

economicBase.value: The trans-Saharan gold, salt and slave trade, plus Niger river agriculture.

tradeRoutes.value: Saharan routes to North Africa, and the Niger River linking Timbuktu, Djenné and Gao.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate. Askia Muhammad carried 300,000 pieces of gold on his pilgrimage (per Cairo historians).

moneyAndTax.value: Cowry shells and gold. Askia Muhammad introduced standard weights and measures.

inequality.value: Nobles and Songhai elites, artisans, and enslaved people (mainly in agriculture).

governmentType.value: A monarchy. Askia Muhammad centralised government with appointed governors over tributary states.

keyRulers.value: Sonni Ali (1464–1492, conqueror). Askia Muhammad the Great (1493–1528). Askia Daoud (1549–1582). Askia Ishaq II (1588–1591/2, last).

succession.value: Disputed: Askia Muhammad seized power from Sonni Ali’s son (1493). His sons later deposed him (1528). Succession wars after 1583.

institutions.value: Islamic law (qadis), standard weights and measures, and provincial governors.

stability.value: A strong state, weakened by succession struggles and a civil war after Askia Daoud’s death (1583).

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between Islamic scholars and Sonni Ali (portrayed as a tyrant by Muslim chroniclers), and between Askia princes.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry and infantry, and a river fleet. It never adopted firearms.

majorWars.value: Sonni Ali’s conquests (Timbuktu 1468, the seven-year siege of Djenné). Wars against the Mossi. The Moroccan invasion and Battle of Tondibi (1591).

territoryChange.value: About 1.4 million km² (1528), falling to 800,000 km² (1550) (Wikipedia infobox).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Mali, the Mossi, the Tuareg and Saadian Morocco.

inventions.value: Dikes and canals for Niger farming (Sonni Ali), and mud-brick architecture (the Tomb of Askia in Gao).

scienceEducation.value: Timbuktu’s Sankore Mosque became a famous centre of learning. Askia Muhammad recruited scholars and supported astronomy.

openness.value: Open to Islamic learning. The army was slow to adopt firearms.

religion.value: Sunni Islam (promoted by the Askias) and traditional African religions (honoured by Sonni Ali).

languageWriting.value: Songhai, Arabic, Tuareg, Mande, Fulani and others. The Timbuktu manuscripts in Arabic.

artsArchitecture.value: The Tomb of Askia (Gao), and the manuscripts and mosques of Timbuktu.

socialStructure.value: Nobles, free people, occupational clans, and enslaved people.

sharedIdentity.value: Songhai identity and Islam among the elite.

neighbours.value: Mali, the Mossi kingdoms, the Hausa states, the Tuareg and Morocco.

ideasReligions.value: Timbuktu attracted scholars from North Africa and Egypt.

colonisation.value: Expanded by conquest over Mali’s former lands.

riseSignals.value: Independence from Mali (c. 1430s), and Sonni Ali’s conquests of Timbuktu and Djenné.

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Askia Muhammad the Great (1493–1528).

declineSignals.value: Succession wars (1528, after 1583), and an army that did not modernise.

outcome.value: Conquest. A Moroccan army with firearms under Judar Pasha defeated Songhai at Tondibi (1591). Nobles fled south and founded the Dendi kingdom.

sources.value: The Timbuktu chronicles (Tarikh al-Sudan, Tarikh al-fattash), Arabic and European accounts. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026.

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Several dates differ between sources (e.g. Djenné 1473 or 1475, start 1464 or 1468).
